rationale: Evidence: all 60 development trials ended off track (0 finishes) at progress 0.09 to 0.19. rms_error was small (0.025 to 0.029 m), but max_error reached about 0.067 m, just past the 0.06 m off-track limit, and every run logged 2 line-loss events. So the robot tracks the line well on average, then loses it during a transient (most likely a curve or a sensor dropout) and departs. The baseline's five sensors span only +/-0.02 m, and the 12 mm footprints leave the outer sensors blind once the robot drifts about 1 cm. Speed (base_speed 1.3) and the lack of damping on sharp bends are the other suspects. Changes: (1) widen the sensor array to seven sensors over +/-0.03 m at 0.01 m spacing, with 16 mm footprints so at least one sensor always sits on the 25 mm tape; (2) keep weights linear in x (scaled to +/-1) so kp keeps its meaning; (3) raise kd from 0.3 to 0.5 to damp the overshoot that causes the max_error peaks; (4) lower base_speed from 1.3 to 1.2 to reduce the lateral transients that push the robot past 6 cm; (5) reduce mass to 0.6 kg for quicker response, with a wider body (0.12 m) to keep the off-track allowance. Expected result: fewer line-loss events and max_error under 0.06, so runs reach progress well above 0.5, though finishing in 3 s may still need a higher speed later. Hypotheses to check next: H1, wider sensor coverage removes the line-loss events; H2, kd 0.5 cuts max_error on the s-bend; H3, the speed needed to finish is about 1.5 m/s, which will need a higher base_speed once the robot stays on the line. Next measurements: line_loss_events, max_error, progress and completion_time, to separate sensing from speed effects.
